idiom_name: attribute composition + context-manager release (weakref for back-references)
implementation_notes: A Python whole is an object whose attributes (or a private list) are its parts; composition and encapsulation are language-level, and classic role classes are unnecessary. Release is the design issue: CPython's reference counting usually frees a whole promptly, but __del__ is not a reliable release path - objects in cycles wait for the cycle collector, finalizers may run during interpreter shutdown, and weakref.finalize is documented to run at exit by default. Deterministic release therefore goes through a context manager: __enter__/__exit__ (or contextlib.closing/ExitStack) around the whole, whose close() cascades to the parts it owns; ExitStack unwinds several optional parts in reverse registration order, and its callbacks are not invoked implicitly when the stack object is garbage collected. Parts that need their whole keep a weakref, and a whole that caches parts or parents a tree uses weak references so the cache never keeps a part alive.
pitfalls: __del__/weakref.finalize ordering is not guaranteed: cycles are collected late, finalizers can fire at shutdown when modules are half torn down, and none of it replaces close() for real resources.
A part holding a strong reference back to its whole (or the whole storing self inside a part) keeps the cycle alive; the back link must be a weakref whose value can legitimately be None.
Handing out the internal list (doc.parts) or mutable part objects lets callers add, replace or close parts behind the whole - expose copies, views or domain methods.
